title: Tech Debt Crisis
narrative:
You're senior now. And the tech debt is real.

The codebase has accumulated 3 years of "quick fixes." Half the tests are flaky. The deployment pipeline takes 45 minutes. New hires quit after a week.

Your manager says: "We need to ship features, not fix old code." But you know: without paying down tech debt, shipping features will get slower and slower.

You need to make the case.

choices.text: Propose a dedicated tech debt sprint

success.text: You present data: tech debt is causing 40% of all bugs. Management agrees to a 2-week cleanup sprint. The team morale improves dramatically.
success.log: Convinced leadership to fund tech debt cleanup!

failure.text: Management says "we'll get to it next quarter." They always say that. You sigh and go back to feature work.

choices.text: Fix it quietly while shipping features

success.text: You refactor small pieces as you go. It's exhausting but the codebase slowly improves. Your team notices.

failure.text: You try to fix things but feature work always takes priority. You're burned out and the codebase is worse than ever.
failure.log: Burned out trying to fix everything.

title: The Interview Panel
narrative:
You're on the engineering interview panel. A candidate is about to come in for a technical interview.

You've been given a coding problem to administer. The problem is... you know it's a terrible problem. It tests trivia, not engineering ability.

The company standard says "use this exact problem." But you know good engineers when you see them.

choices.text: Use the standard problem but adapt it

success.text: You follow the letter of the policy but add real-world context. The candidate shines. You hire them. They become a great teammate.

failure.text: The candidate is good but the problem doesn't showcase their strengths. They perform poorly. You reject them. Two months later, a competitor hires them as a senior.
failure.log: Rejected a good candidate. Bad hire decision.

choices.text: Reject the standard problem and design your own

success.text: You design a realistic system design exercise. The candidate loves it. They show their true abilities. You hire them.
success.log: Better interview process led to great hire!

failure.text: Your manager says you broke protocol. The candidate is confused by your unstructured format. Nobody's happy.

title: Burnout Warning Signs
narrative:
You've been working 60+ hour weeks for 3 months. Your code quality is slipping. You're irritable in meetings. You check Slack in your dreams.

Your doctor says: "You need to reduce stress." Your partner says: "You need to be present." Your team lead says: "We're worried about you."

But there's a major release next week.

choices.text: Take a week off. Unplug completely.

success.text: You hand off your responsibilities. The team manages fine. You come back refreshed and your code quality doubles. Your team respects you for prioritizing health.
success.log: Took time off. Came back stronger!

failure.text: You try to disconnect but the release needs you. You spend the week "off" answering Slack messages. It's the worst of both worlds.

success.text: You delegate effectively and say "no" to non-essential work. Your team steps up. You maintain work-life balance and the release ships.

failure.text: You try to delegate but nobody else knows the system. You end up doing more work teaching others. The release is stressful.

choices.text: Push through. It's just one more release.

success.text: Against all odds, you power through. The release ships. But you're running on fumes. The victory feels hollow.
success.log: Survived the release but at a cost.

failure.text: You collapse. Not dramatically — just a bad week of illness. The release is delayed. Your team covers for you but trust is damaged.

title: Performance Review
narrative:
It's performance review season. Your manager calls you into a meeting (or Zoom call). They have a document.

"Let's talk about your year. You've delivered well on most projects. Your code quality has improved. However..."

The "however" is coming.

success.text: You present a well-documented list of achievements. Your manager is impressed. You get a strong rating and a raise.

failure.text: You wing it. Your manager has a different view of your year. The rating is lower than expected.

success.text: You get candid, useful feedback. You create a growth plan. Your manager respects your maturity.

failure.text: The feedback is harsh and unconstructive. "You need more visibility." Translation: "You need to be more political."

title: Conference Talk Opportunity
narrative:
Your company is sending 3 people to a major tech conference. Your manager asks who wants to go and present.

Public speaking terrifies you. But it's a career opportunity. The conference has 5,000 attendees and industry leaders.

Your coworker who loves attention is also interested.

success.text: You practice for weeks. Your talk is excellent. You meet industry leaders. Your career gets a huge boost.

failure.text: You freeze on stage. It's awkward. But... people were kind. You learn and come back stronger next year.
failure.log: Conference talk was rough but you learned.

success.text: Your coworker absolutely crushes it. They thank you for the opportunity. You look like a team player.

failure.text: Your coworker steals your thunder. They mention your work in their talk and get all the credit. You're not mad. (You're a little mad.)

title: The Promotion Review
narrative:
It's promotion review season. You're up for Senior → Staff.

Your manager says: "You need more visibility. You need to influence at a higher level. You need to..."

You look at your coworker who just gave a talk at a major conference. They're already getting their promotion packet.

You've spent 6 months deep in the code. Nobody knows what you've built.

success.text: You write a compelling report showing your impact. Your manager is impressed. You get the promotion.

failure.text: Your report is too technical. Your manager doesn't understand it. You wait another quarter.

choices.text: Start giving talks and writing blog posts

success.text: You give a talk at an internal tech day. People are impressed. You get invited to speak externally.

failure.text: Nobody shows up to your talk. 3 people attend. One is your manager.

title: The Security Audit
narrative:
The security team just finished their audit. Your service has 237 vulnerabilities. 12 are critical.

The worst one: your API keys are hardcoded in the source code. They've been public on GitHub for 6 months.

The CISO wants a meeting. Tomorrow.

success.text: You admit the mistakes and present a remediation plan. The CISO respects your honesty. You fix everything in 2 weeks.

failure.text: The CISO is furious. They want your head. You're assigned to security work for the next 6 months.

success.text: You blame the legacy codebase. The CISO buys it. You get a pass. (You're a little ashamed.)

failure.text: The CISO knows you wrote the code. They don't buy the excuse. You're in trouble.

title: The Keynote Invitation
narrative:
You've been invited to give a keynote at a major tech conference. 3,000 attendees. Industry leaders in the audience.

Your topic: "How we scaled our platform to 10 million users."

You've never given a keynote. You've barely given a talk.

Your hands are shaking.

choices.text: Practice like your life depends on it

success.text: You practice for weeks. The keynote is a hit. People approach you after with job offers.

failure.text: You freeze on stage. It's painful. But people were kind. You learn and come back stronger.
failure.log: Freeze on stage. But you learned.

success.text: The coach helps you find your voice. The keynote is great. You're a natural.
success.log: Speaker coach made you a pro!

failure.text: The coach is a scam. You waste $5,000 and still freeze on stage.

title: The KPI Trap
narrative:
Your manager introduces new KPIs: lines of code committed, PRs merged per week, tickets closed.

You've been writing careful, well-tested code. This will make you look bad.

Your coworker who writes spaghetti code is now the top performer.

The CEO loves the dashboard.

success.text: You present data showing KPIs don't correlate with quality. Your manager listens. KPIs are changed.

failure.text: Your manager says "the CEO loves the dashboard." You're told to adapt.

success.text: You break features into tiny PRs. Your KPIs look great. You feel dirty but you're #1.

failure.text: Your manager notices the tiny PRs. They ask why you're not shipping features.

title: The On-Call Nightmare
narrative:
It's your on-call week. Your phone buzzes at 3 AM.

"Database is down. Users can't log in. The CEO is calling."

You've been on-call for 3 weeks straight. You're exhausted.

The database cluster has 47 nodes. You don't know which one is failing.

success.text: You methodically check each node. You find the failing one. You restart it. Database recovers.

failure.text: You check nodes randomly. You waste 2 hours. The CEO calls again.

success.text: The DBA team fixes it in 15 minutes. You learn the root cause. You're on-call again next week.

failure.text: The DBA team is asleep. You wait 45 minutes. The CEO is furious.

title: The Blameless Retrospective
narrative:
A production incident just happened. Your team is in a retrospective.

The manager says: "This is a blameless retrospective. Let's focus on process, not people."

But everyone is looking at you. You deployed the bad code. You missed the test. You should have caught it.

The silence is deafening.

success.text: You admit your mistake and propose process improvements. Your team respects your honesty.
success.log: Owned the mistake. Team respected you!

failure.text: You admit your mistake but your manager takes it too far. They make it about you, not process.

choices.text: Stay quiet and let it pass

success.text: Nobody mentions you. The retrospective moves on. You learn privately.

failure.text: Your coworker mentions you. "John deployed the bad code." The room turns to you.

title: The Architecture Presentation
narrative:
You've designed a new architecture. It's elegant, scalable, and perfect.

You're presenting it to the engineering team. They have questions.

"What about latency?" "What about cost?" "What about our existing infrastructure?"

You didn't think about those.

choices.text: Admit you didn't consider those factors

success.text: You admit the gaps. The team helps you fill them. The architecture gets better.

failure.text: You deflect. The team doesn't buy it. Your credibility takes a hit.

success.text: You address each concern with data. The team is convinced. The architecture ships.

failure.text: Your data is weak. The team pushes back harder. The architecture is delayed.

title: The SVPG Product Model
narrative:
Your company is adopting the Silicon Valley Product Group (SVPG) model. The VP of Product just sent a 47-page deck.

It talks about "product-market fit," "the product lifecycle," and "the three horizons."

You don't know what any of this means. Your team lead says it means "product wants more features."

The new process: every feature needs a "Product Requirements Document" AND a "Success Metrics Framework" AND a "Go-to-Market Alignment."

Your simple bug fix now needs a 10-page doc.

success.text: You read the deck. You understand the SVPG model. You write a PRD that actually helps. Product respects you.

failure.text: You read the deck. You don't understand it. You write a 10-page PRD that nobody reads.

success.text: You write a 2-page PRD. Product complains but approves it. You ship faster than everyone else.

failure.text: Product rejects your 2-page PRD. They want 10 pages. You're stuck in review for 2 weeks.

title: The Product Triangle
narrative:
Your VP of Product introduces the "Product Triangle": Fast, Good, Cheap. Pick two.

They say: "We want Fast AND Good. We're sorry, it's going to be expensive."

Your budget is cut 30%.

Your team lead says: "Just make it work."

The product team says: "We need it in 2 weeks."

The CEO says: "Make it great."

The Product Triangle is... a lie.

success.text: You draw the triangle on a whiteboard. Everyone understands. They pick "Good and Cheap" and give you more time.

failure.text: The VP says "we're special. We can break the triangle." Nobody believes them.

success.text: You build it. It's fast, it's good, and it's expensive. Your team burns out but ships.

failure.text: You can't make it work. The feature ships late, it's buggy, and it costs more than expected.

title: The Code of Conduct Incident
narrative:
A team member makes an inappropriate comment in a public channel. It's not terrible, but it's not okay.

The team is divided. Some think it's no big deal. Others are offended.

Your manager says: "Handle this. You're a senior engineer."

It's your call.

success.text: You talk to them privately. They apologize. The team moves on. Everyone respects your handling.
success.log: Handled it privately. Team respected you!

failure.text: You address it publicly. They get defensive. The situation gets worse.

success.text: HR handles it professionally. You're not involved. The team moves on.

failure.text: HR takes 2 weeks. The team is simmering. Your manager asks why you didn't step in.

title: BOSS: The Platform Rewrite
narrative:
Your BOSS. The CTO has declared the entire platform "architecturally unsound" and wants a complete rewrite in a new stack.

"The old system was built by amateurs," they say. (It was built by you and your team over 3 years.)

You're tasked with building the new platform. The old system has 2 million users. Downtime is NOT an option.

The rewrite challenge awaits.

choices.text: Build it right — proper architecture, proper testing

success.text: You design a beautiful, scalable architecture. The new platform is 10x faster, 10x more reliable. It takes 6 months but it's worth it. You've proven the old system's worth by building something even better.
success.log: Built a platform that outshines the old one!

failure.text: Perfection takes too long. The old system is still breaking while you're building the perfect new one. Leadership gets impatient.

choices.text: Ship a minimal viable platform and iterate

success.text: You ship the basics in 2 months. It's not perfect but it works. You iterate based on real usage. Leadership is impressed by the speed.

failure.text: The MVP is too minimal. It can't handle production load. You have to rebuild significant portions. Now you have TWO platforms.

choices.text: Push back — the old system works fine

success.text: You present data showing the old system is stable. You propose incremental improvements instead of a rewrite. The CTO backs down. Crisis averted.

failure.text: The CTO is unmoved. "I've made my decision." You're stuck leading a rewrite you think is unnecessary. Morale plummets.
